records.text: Look at that: one piece attacking several targets at the same moment. A fork, and a very busy piece.
Curious how much one enemy piece could do from here. A fork is now possible for the other side, with several targets under attack at once.
Another move contained a fork, one piece hitting several targets together. This move goes a different way and leaves it unused.
Interesting. This piece looks free, yet it is pinned to its king. Move it off the line and the king is exposed, so it is stuck where it is.
Now a pin to the king becomes possible for the other side. A piece caught that way is stuck: stepping off the line would expose its own king.
A different move would have fixed an enemy piece to its king, since leaving the line would have exposed the king. A pin, unplayed.
A skewer. The front piece is attacked, and when it steps away, the piece behind it on the same line is exposed. Two targets, arranged in a queue.
This permits a skewer. If the front piece is forced off the line, the piece behind it is exposed.
A stronger move had a skewer in it: attack the front piece, and once it moves aside, the one behind it is exposed.
The point is to capture a defender. Watch what that defender was protecting; that is what loses its cover.
Now the other side can capture a defender, and whatever it protected may be left without cover.
Another move could have captured a defender, stripping the protection from whatever it guarded.
Fascinating, really: the king is shut in by its own pieces. That is the back-rank mate.
This opens a route to a back-rank mate for the other side. The king's own pieces are the ones blocking its escape.
There was a back-rank mate available, the enemy king trapped behind its own pieces. This move does not take it.
The idea is promotion: bring the pawn all the way to the last rank, where it becomes a new piece. Such a small piece, with such a large future.
This gives the other side a chance to promote. One of their pawns could reach the last rank and turn into a new piece.
A stronger move offered a route to promotion. This move leaves that pawn short of the last rank.
A discovered attack. The moving piece clears the way; the real attack comes from the piece that was hidden behind it, along the newly opened line.
A discovered attack is now possible: one piece moves aside, and a threat appears from the piece behind it.
Another move had a discovered attack in it: move one piece aside, and a threat appears from the piece behind.
Two threats launched by one move: a double attack. The defense now has two problems to solve at once.
A double attack becomes available to the other side: one move, two threats.
A stronger move contained a double attack, two threats in one move. This move does not find it.
A deflection. The defender is drawn away from its duty, and what it was guarding is left exposed.
This gives the other side a chance at a deflection, pulling a defender away from its task, so whatever it guarded is left open.
Another move could have pulled a defender away from its duty. That deflection would have left what it guarded uncovered.
Before anything clever, check for pieces with no defender. Here there is one, and the idea is simply to take it.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece. This one passes over it, and nothing was guarding it at all.
After this move, one piece has no defender, and the other side can take it.
A convincing move on its own, but it removes a piece's only real defender. Now the other side can capture the piece that was left behind.
The opponent's previous move carried a threat, and this one does not respond to it. A piece can now be captured.
This capture invites a recapture of a more valuable piece. An exchange is only finished when both captures are counted.
A minor piece leaves its starting square and enters the game. Development, plainly visible.
A different move would have developed a minor piece, bringing it off its starting square.
An open file, and the rook is on it. From one end to the other, no pawn of either color.
Another move would have placed a rook on an open file, one with no pawns of either color.
A semi-open file for the rook: no friendly pawn on it, though an enemy pawn is still somewhere along it.
A different move would have placed a rook on a semi-open file: no friendly pawn on it, but at least one enemy pawn.
A passed pawn. Look along its file and both neighboring files: no enemy pawn stands ahead.
Another move would have created a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead on its file or the neighboring files.
The pawn was already passed, and this move pushes it further forward. Each step brings it nearer the last rank.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn further up the board.
This leaves an isolated pawn. No friendly pawn stands on either neighboring file.
A different move would have left an isolated pawn, lacking any friendly pawn on the neighboring files.
Before this move, a piece stood undefended. Now a defender covers it. A new connection on the board.
Another move would have given an undefended piece a defender.
This leaves a piece without a defender. Undefended describes the piece; it does not prove the piece can be won.
Another move would have left a piece undefended, though that alone would not mean it could be won.
A new legal square for the king to step to, opened by this move. A small exit, newly made.
A different move would have given the king a new flight square.
The king castles, and the rook crosses over beside it. Two pieces relocated in one move.
Castling was the alternative: king and rook relocated in one move.
With this capture, a bishop pair is broken. The side that lost the bishop now covers only one square color with bishops.
A different move would have captured a bishop, breaking the other side's bishop pair.
Doubled pawns: two pawns of one color now share a file.
With a different move, two pawns of one color would have ended up on a single file: doubled pawns.
With this move, a forced checkmate opens up for the other side. The path of that attack is worth tracing, move by move.
The finish was there: a forced checkmate with another move. This one goes past it. That mate is worth finding now.
The material looks lost, and yet the sacrifice holds. In the line that was checked, accepting it does not refute the idea.
A very narrow margin. Among all the moves checked, this was the single one that kept the position playable; the rest were losing.
Only this move kept the advantage. Among the moves checked, every other choice was losing.
The reply comes at once: the other side can capture something immediately.
The strongest reply is a check, and the king has to be dealt with before anything else.
The engine prefers another move here. Play it on the board and compare what the replies do.
By the engine's measure, this move is weaker than the best option. The reply shows where the difference appears.
Strong. Among the moves the engine examined, this one stands up well.
A sound move. It keeps much of what the position offered, even if the engine has another first choice.
This is what fascinates me. The human-move model finds this a natural choice, and the engine still finds something stronger. What looks right and what works can differ.
Unusual, by the human-move model's estimate, and strong by the engine's. Unfamiliar is not the same as wrong.
The engine found exactly one move that kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it difficult to find. The gap between the right move and the findable one interests me.
By the human-move model and the alternatives, this was a hard move to find. The right answer and the obvious one were not the same here.
A hard-to-find defense, by the human-move model and the alternatives, and it kept the position playable. Exactly the kind of moment I like to study.
Natural to the human-move model, and the engine's best move too. Instinct and calculation agree here.
A natural choice by the human-move model, and a strong one by the engine, although the engine prefers another move.
The recorded clock shows very little time left before this move. That belongs beside everything else on the board.
By the recorded clock, a quick move, with time still in hand.
The recorded clock shows a long deliberation on this move.
This move appears in the opening catalogue, part of a documented line.
Here the game steps off the documented opening line for the first time. From this move on, it is its own.
After the earlier setback, the position is playable again with this move. An earlier error, not a final one.
This brings back a playable position after the earlier setback, and errors from the other side helped make it possible.
The opponent's previous move offered a chance, and this move uses it. One side's lapse, the other side's opportunity.
The opponent's last move offered an opportunity, and this move passes over it. A stronger answer was available.
This same issue has appeared earlier in this game. When something repeats, I start paying closer attention. Compare the moments where it appeared.
Earlier, this piece was left unguarded. Now it has a defender again.
No single move did the damage here. This is one of several small concessions that, together, have worsened the position.
The advantage was kept through the reviewed moves, right through to the recorded win. That stretch shows how an edge is held.
This issue also shows up in other saved games. Collected together, those examples say more than any one of them alone.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape left. Every exit closed, and the attack complete.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape. The decisions worth examining come earlier, before the attack arrived.
The game ends in a draw. A settled result, though the decisions along the way are still worth examining.
I'll watch with interest. Study the position, then choose your move.
That attempt does not stand up. Look again and try another move.
That attempt produced no result. Return to the move and try once more.
The saved engine analysis shows a forced checkmate for the side that played this move.
The saved engine analysis shows the other side with a forced checkmate after this move.
Count the material along the saved line: the side that played this move comes out ahead of where it started.
Count the material along the saved line: the side that played this move comes out behind where it started.
This move is accepted for the exercise, though the moves shown give no clear tactical explanation. Accepted, and still a small mystery.
This move is not accepted for the exercise, and the moves shown give no clear tactical reason for that.
This move matches one of the saved answers, and for this exercise the saved answers are what decide acceptance.
This move falls outside the saved answers for the exercise. Outside the answers is not the same as bad chess.
Examine the move closely, then go on to the next position.
Good move. Remember why it works, not only what it was.
Practice saved. Nothing about your review schedule has changed.
Solved. This recall remains marked for relearning.
This is the starting position, before any of the moves under examination.
The next move. Observe what has changed.
This move gives check, so the king's safety must be answered first.
With this move, the king escapes the check.
Last rank reached; the pawn promotes. A pawn no longer.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes, giving check at the same time.
The pawn reaches the last rank and promotes, and it is checkmate. The king has no legal escape.
Promotion on the last rank, and with the same move, its king is no longer in check.
A capture: one piece is removed from the board.
A capture that also gives check. Two things accomplished by one move.
This capture is also checkmate. The king has no legal escape.
This capture removes the check on its own king as well.
A pawn capture on the last rank, and promotion on the same square.
One pawn move does three things: it captures on the last rank, promotes, and gives check.
The pawn captures on the last rank, promotes, and with that, checkmate: every legal escape for the king is gone.
A capture on the last rank, a promotion, and the end of the check against its own king, all from one pawn move.
The king castles, the rook crosses over, and the move gives check as well.
The king castles, the rook crosses over, and it is checkmate. The other king has no legal escape. A rare way to finish, and a memorable one.
Follow the forking piece: it attacks several targets at once, then collects one. The example also shows a net material gain.
The piece cannot make the indicated capture, because it is pinned to its king. Stepping off the pin line would expose the king.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king, so it cannot simply run. Only moves that keep the king shielded are allowed.
The defenders are pinned to their king, so they cannot recapture there; that is why the capture works. The line shown includes a material gain.
Observe the pinned piece. It cannot leave its line without exposing its king, and as these moves unfold, it is captured.
The front piece moves off the line, and the piece it was screening is captured along that same line.
Here the king is in check along the line and has to step away. Once it does, the same attacker collects the piece that stood behind it.
The captures come in order: first the only defender, then the piece it guarded. The first capture is what makes the second one possible.
The defender is drawn away from its duty, and the piece it was guarding is then captured.
The blocker steps aside, the piece behind it gains a line, and it makes the capture along that line.
The moving piece clears the way, and check comes from a different piece behind it.
Double check: two pieces attack the king at the same instant. Remarkable, the efficiency of it.
The first piece makes its own attack and opens a line for another. In this example, that second piece captures its target.
Follow the pawn until it promotes. In this example, that side also finishes with a net material gain.
The undefended piece is captured, and in this example the capturing side comes away with a net material gain.
The opponent's previous move released a relative pin on the attacking piece. After the next move the target was still standing there, and in the shown line it is captured.
The other side has a legal reply, marked on the board. Make it there and observe what follows.
Before moving, check which of your pieces could be captured with no useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, look for enemy pieces that are not defended.
Look at forcing moves where one piece attacks two valuable targets together.
Before moving a pinned piece, see what stands behind it: your king, or a more valuable piece.
Look beyond the first target. An attack along the line can expose a more valuable piece behind it.
Before exchanging a defender, find out what it is protecting at the moment.
Notice which lines open when a blocking piece moves away.
Search for a single move that makes two threats, counting checks and newly opened lines.
Before moving a back-rank defender, look at the king's escape squares.
Count the moves the pawn needs to promote, and look at the forcing pawn advances.
Before moving a defender, see which pieces would lose its protection.
An exchange has two parts: what you capture, and what their recapture takes back. Count both before judging.
Check whether a forcing exchange could pull a defender away from another target.
For this exercise, the saved answers set the rule. Another legal move is not necessarily bad chess.
The moves shown answer each turn with a strong reply; none of those replies is necessarily forced.
These material changes belong to the shown line only, counted from where it began. The written explanation gives the piece values.
The saved line holds no simple tactical reason. Play through it and set the replies against each other; no positional explanation has been assumed.
This explanation uses the answer policy saved for the exercise. The written notes show its setting.

The full solution, with no wrong moves. Fascinating to watch it found so cleanly.

Book. This move is part of a catalogued opening line.
Still within the documented opening.
Another move the catalogue has on record.
The reply is in the book too.
The catalogued line goes on.
Still documented. Nothing new to the catalogue yet.
Another step along the documented line.
This one has a book entry as well.
Book once more. The catalogue records what was played, not whether it was right.
A convincing move, and the human-move model agrees it is natural. Yet after it, the other side can force checkmate. Follow how the attack reaches the king.
The human-move model calls this a natural choice. Meanwhile another move had a forced checkmate, and this one lets it go. Go back and find that finish.
It looks ordinary, and the human-move model expects it. But the other side can capture something straight away; start with that reply.
This is the contrast I find fascinating. The human-move model sees a natural move; the engine rates it below the best option. The replies show where the appealing choice loses value.
Natural, by the human-move model, yet it opens a fork for the other side, one of their pieces attacking several targets at once. How a move looks and what it allows are two different measurements.
A likely choice for the human-move model, but it allows a skewer. If the front piece is forced to move, the piece behind it on that line is exposed.
Remarkable. Every other checked move was losing; only this one kept the position playable. The human-move model rates it hard to find, and still you found it.
The single move among those checked that kept the position playable; everything else was losing. The human-move model and the alternatives both suggest it was hard to find.
The advantage survives, and only because of this move: every other checked choice was losing. The human-move model marks it as hard to find, and it was found.
Only this move kept the advantage, and every other one checked was losing. The human-move model suggests it was hard to find. The rare move, and the right one.
Not a move the human-move model expects, yet the engine calls it strong. A single piece now attacks several targets: a fork.
A fork, and the engine's first choice, one piece attacking several targets together. By the human-move model and the alternatives, it was hard to find. I do enjoy a gap like that.
Unusual, says the human-move model. Strong, says the engine. Between the two sits a pin to the king, holding a piece on its line.
The engine's best move, and a hard one to find by the human-move model. It pins a piece to its king, and that piece cannot step off the line without exposing the king.
At a glance, convincing, and the human-move model rates it natural. Look closer: the move pulls away the only real defender of a piece, and the other side can capture it.
The move pulls the only real defender away, and the piece it was guarding can now be captured. A single checked move would have held the position; the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
The human-move model finds this natural, but the opponent's previous move had made a threat, and this leaves it unanswered. A piece can now be captured.

The threat arrived with the opponent's last move, and this leaves it unanswered, so a piece can be captured. One defense among the moves checked kept things playable; the human-move model marks it as difficult.
Taking is natural, by the human-move model. The reply, though, takes back a more valuable piece. An exchange is judged by both captures, never the first alone.
The capture invites a recapture of something more valuable. A different move, the only checked one that held the position, was what mattered, and the human-move model suggests it was well hidden.
One piece, several targets under attack together: a fork. Here the human-move model and the engine are in perfect accord, natural and best. The obvious move and the correct one coincide.
There is a fork in this move, one piece attacking several targets. Natural, by the human-move model; strong, by the engine, which still ranks something else first.
Now a fork is available to the other side, one piece reaching several targets. Exactly one checked move would have kept the position playable; the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
Another move contained a fork, one piece hitting several targets at once. The played move is the natural one, by the human-move model, and it leaves that fork unused.
Of every move checked, a single one held the position, and it contained a fork, one piece hitting several targets. It was missed; by the human-move model, it was hard to see.
Natural for the human-move model and the engine's top move: a pin to the king, which leaves the pinned piece unable to step off the line.
A pin to the king, in a move the human-move model finds natural; the pinned piece cannot leave the line without exposing its king. Strong, although the engine has another first choice.
The human-move model finds the move natural. The trouble is what it allows: a pin to the king, after which the pinned piece is stuck on its line, unable to move without exposing its king.
This allows a pin to the king. Just one checked move kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates that defense hard to find.
A different move would have pinned an enemy piece to its king, freezing it on its line. The human-move model expected the move that was actually played, and the pin never came.
The one checked move that kept the position playable involved a pin to the king. It went unplayed, and the human-move model marks it a difficult find.
A skewer: attack the front piece, and when it moves aside, the one behind it is exposed. The engine's best move, and by the human-move model, a hard one to find.
The human-move model did not expect it, and the engine rates it strong. There is a skewer here, the front piece moving aside to expose the one behind. Unfamiliar is not the same as weak.
Natural and best together: the human-move model expects it, and the engine ranks it first. The idea is a skewer, exposing the piece behind the front one.
There is a skewer in this move: once the front piece gives way, whatever stands behind it is exposed. Natural, by the human-move model; strong, if not the engine's first pick.

Now the other side has a skewer available: the front piece is attacked, and if it steps away, the piece behind it falls exposed. One checked move held the position, and the human-move model marks it as hard to see.
Another move held a skewer, the front piece forced aside to expose the one behind. The played move is natural to the human-move model, yet it misses that line.
Among the moves checked, the single one that held contained a skewer, forcing a front piece aside to expose another behind it. It was missed, and the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
The idea is to capture a defender, so that what it guarded loses its protection. The engine's top choice, and a hard find according to the human-move model.
The human-move model would not have predicted this, and the engine judges it strong. The point is to capture a defender and remove the protection it gave.
Natural to the human-move model and best for the engine. Capture the defender, and whatever it was protecting loses its cover.
A natural move, in the human-move model's estimate, that captures a defender, so whatever it guarded loses protection. Strong, with one engine preference above it.
Natural, according to the human-move model, but it lets the other side capture a defender, leaving whatever it guarded without protection.
The other side can now capture a defender, and what it guards could lose protection. One move among those checked held the position, and the human-move model rates it hard to see.
Another move could have captured a defender and removed its protection. The move played is the natural one by the human-move model, and the defender stays where it is.
One checked move kept the position playable, and it captured a defender, stripping away its protection. It was not played; the human-move model suggests it was hard to find.
The king is trapped by its own pieces: a back-rank mating idea. The engine ranks the move best, and the human-move model and the alternatives point to a hard find.
Unusual, by the human-move model; strong, by the engine; and the idea is a back-rank mate, the king boxed in by its own pieces. Three facts, and I like all of them.
A back-rank mating idea, the king's own pieces blocking its escape. The human-move model finds it natural, and the engine ranks it best.
Strong, and it carries the back-rank mating idea: the king trapped by its own pieces. The human-move model finds it natural, though the engine has another favorite.
The idea is promotion: bring the pawn to the last rank and turn it into a new piece. The engine's first choice, and hard to find by the human-move model.
Unexpected to the human-move model, and strong by the engine. The point is promotion, a pawn reaching the last rank to become a new piece.
A pawn is given its route to the last rank and promotion, and the human-move model expects the move while the engine ranks it best.
A natural move with promotion as its aim, a pawn heading for the last rank. Strong, though the engine places another move above it.
Natural, by the human-move model, yet it gives the other side a chance to promote: one of their pawns could reach the last rank.
This opens a path to promotion for one of the other side's pawns. A single checked move kept the position playable; the human-move model rates it a difficult find.
The natural move, by the human-move model's estimate, and yet a different move would have marched a pawn toward promotion. That route stays unused.
The single move that held the position, among those checked, would have pushed a pawn toward promotion. It stayed unplayed, and the human-move model rates it a difficult find.
The piece in front moves, and the attack arrives from the piece behind: a discovered attack. It is the engine's top choice, and the human-move model marks it difficult.
Surprising to the human-move model, strong by the engine. The front piece moves away and reveals an attack from the piece behind it, a discovered attack.
A discovered attack, and both judges agree on it: natural for the human-move model, first for the engine. The front piece moves, and the piece behind it attacks.
A natural move, by the human-move model's estimate, that clears a line: a discovered attack from the piece behind. Strong, with the engine leaning toward something else.
It looks natural, and the human-move model agrees. Yet now a piece of theirs can step off its line and uncover a threat from the piece behind: a discovered attack.

This permits a discovered attack, a piece stepping off a line so that the one behind it can threaten. One defense among the moves checked would have held, and the human-move model marks it as difficult.
Another move had a discovered attack in it, a piece stepping aside to uncover a threat behind. The played move is the natural one for the human-move model, and the line stays closed.
The single checked move that kept the position playable used a discovered attack. It was missed, and the human-move model suggests it was hard to see.
Two threats from one move, a double attack, and the engine's best. The human-move model and the alternatives suggest it was hard to find.
Two threats from one move: a double attack. Unusual, by the human-move model's estimate, and strong by the engine's. Unexpected and strong, a pairing I never tire of.
Two threats at once, and the obvious move happens to be the best one: natural to the human-move model, first for the engine.
A double attack in a natural move, two threats with a single stroke. Strong by the engine, which still prefers something else.
Natural, by the human-move model, yet it gives the other side a double attack, two threats arriving with a single move.
Two threats from one enemy move become possible: a double attack. Among the moves checked, a single one held, and the human-move model suggests it was not easy to find.
Another move contained a double attack, two threats in one. The move played is natural to the human-move model, but it leaves that double threat unplayed.
The only checked move that kept the position playable made two threats at once. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates it a difficult find.
A deflection: the defender is pulled away from its duty, and what it guarded is left exposed. The engine's first choice, and a hard one by the human-move model.
Unusual, by the human-move model; strong, by the engine. A deflection draws a defender off its task, leaving what it guarded open.
Natural and best: the human-move model expects it, and the engine agrees it is the top move. The idea is a deflection, drawing a defender away from what it protects.
A natural move that deflects a defender, pulling it off what it guarded. Strong, though the engine has a different first choice.
Natural, by the human-move model, but it gives the other side a deflection: a defender pulled away, and what it guarded left open.

A piece with no defender, simply taken. And yet, by the human-move model and the alternatives, it was hard to find. The engine ranks it best. A strange pairing, and a fascinating one.
Taking an undefended piece, with a move the human-move model finds unusual. Strong, by the engine's measure. Rare and right, both at once.
An undefended piece, and the natural move takes it. The human-move model expects it, and the engine ranks it best.
The move takes an undefended piece, and the human-move model finds it natural. Strong, although the engine prefers something else.
Another move could have taken an undefended piece. The played move is natural to the human-move model, but that loose piece stays on the board.
The only checked move that kept the position playable took an undefended piece. It was missed, and the human-move model suggests it was hard to see.
A natural move by the human-move model, and it leaves a piece without a defender. The other side can simply take it.
This leaves a piece with no defender at all, ready to be taken. Among the moves checked, a single one would have held, and by the human-move model's reckoning it was difficult.
A minor piece leaves its starting square. A quiet move, and yet the engine ranks it best and the human-move model suggests it was hard to find. Quiet moves can hide well.
Development, by an unusual route: the human-move model did not expect this minor piece to come out, but the engine finds the move strong.
A minor piece comes off its starting square, natural to the human-move model and the engine's best. Nothing hidden here, just the correct move.

The rook takes an open file, empty of pawns. The human-move model expects it, and the engine ranks it first.
A natural move that puts the rook on an open file, free of pawns. Strong, though the engine has a favorite of its own.
The rook goes to a semi-open file: none of its own pawns there, an enemy pawn still ahead. The engine's best move, and not an easy one to find, by the human-move model.

A semi-open file for the rook, no friendly pawns on it, at least one enemy pawn. Natural, by the human-move model, and the engine's best.
The rook settles on a semi-open file with enemy pawns still on it. The human-move model finds the move natural, and the engine strong, though not its first choice.
